curriculumDefinition.commandsAndConcepts: `:normal`, `:normal!`; range and visual application; `:global`/`:g`; `:vglobal`/`:v`; global delete, substitute, normal commands, and macros; `:copy`/`:move` relocation by predicate; previewing a predicate before it runs; undo grouping; combined predicates and transformations
curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Apply Normal-mode edits across a controlled line set, relocate matching lines, and choose the lowest-risk automation mechanism
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Run a text-object edit on selected lines; delete debug lines; modify only declarations matching a predicate; execute a macro over matches; gather matching lines at a chosen address
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core advanced automation. The distinction between mapped and unmapped Normal commands is explained, while mappings themselves stay out of scope

lessons.title: Delete lines by predicate
lessons.objective: Use `:global` to remove only lines matching a pattern.

activities.title: Run an Ex command on matching lines
activities.body: `:global` (or `:g`) finds lines that match a pattern, then runs an Ex command on each one. Without a range, it checks the whole file. Confirm the pattern with a search or a counting substitution first: the marks show which lines it selects, including the ones outside the window.
activities.contrast: The `g` in `:global` selects lines; it is unrelated to the `g` substitution flag. Preview before deleting, because the matches you cannot see are deleted too.

lessons.title: Collect and reorder by predicate
lessons.objective: Copy or move every matching line to a chosen address.

activities.title: Send matching lines somewhere else
activities.body: The command nested inside `:global` can take an address instead of editing text. `:t{addr}` copies each matching line below that address and `:m{addr}` moves it, so one predicate can gather scattered lines into a block.
activities.contrast: `$` grows as lines arrive, so the block keeps its order; `0` never moves, so every match lands above the last one and the block arrives reversed.

activities.title: Gather every matching row
activities.instruction: Copy every ERROR row to the end of the buffer, leaving the originals in place.

commandGroups.explanation: Choose matching lines and copy each one to the address that follows.

hints: The nested command can be an address-taking command, not only an edit.
`:t` copies the current line below an address.
Use `:g/ERROR/t$`.

feedback.success: Every match now has a copy collected at the end.
feedback.why: The predicate chose the lines and `:t$` sent a copy of each one below the last line, in the order they were found.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log makes a scattered severity predicate and a gathered summary immediately readable.

activities.title: Move matches to the end
activities.instruction: Relocate every WARN row to the end of the buffer, keeping their original order.

commandGroups.explanation: Choose matching lines and move each one to the address that follows.

hints: Moving differs from copying only in whether the original stays.
An address of `$` appends after the last line, which grows as the run proceeds.
Use `:g/WARN/m$`.

feedback.success: The warnings are collected at the end in their original order.
feedback.why: Each match is appended after the previous one, so a trailing address preserves the order the predicate found them in.

activities.portability: Defined and conformance-tested Vim Wilds behavior, matching native Vim for this fixture.

provenance.languageRationale: log keeps severity a plain text predicate, so the reorder is the only thing to read.

activities.title: Hoist matches to the top
activities.instruction: Relocate every import to the top of the file and note the order they arrive in.

commandGroups.explanation: Choose matching lines and move each one above the first line.

hints: A fixed address does not move as the run proceeds.
Every match lands at the same place, ahead of the ones already moved.
Use `:g/^import/m0`.

feedback.success: The imports are hoisted, and their order is reversed.
feedback.why: `0` never moves, so each match is inserted above the previous one and the block arrives back to front. `$` grows with the buffer, which is why it preserves order.

lessons.title: Choose the lowest-risk automation
lessons.objective: Select among ranges, predicates, substitutions, Normal commands, and macros.

activities.title: Choose the simplest automation for the task
activities.body: Use a range for known lines, substitution for direct text replacement, `:normal` for one structural edit, `:global` to choose lines by text, and a macro for a true multi-step edit. Weigh the cost of reversing too: a whole `:global` run undoes in one step, while a macro replayed ten times takes ten.
activities.contrast: Advanced commands are valuable because they clarify intent, not because they are advanced.

activities.title: Reverse a whole run
activities.instruction: Delete every DEBUG row, then put the buffer back exactly as it was.

commandGroups.explanation: Choose matching lines and enter the operation to apply to them.
Undo the whole run. One step reverses every line the command touched.

hints: Count the undo steps a mechanism costs before you run it.
A `:global` run is a single change, however many lines it touched.
Run `:g/DEBUG/d`, then press `u` once.

feedback.success: One undo reversed every deleted row.
feedback.why: A whole `:global` run is one change, so it costs one `u`. A macro replayed ten times is ten changes and costs ten.

activities.title: Choose the simplest safe mechanism
activities.prompt: The same short Normal-mode edit must run on lines 12 through 15, and those line numbers are already verified. What should you start with?

options.label: A `:global` command that replays a macro

activities.explanation: A known contiguous line set plus one local Normal command needs neither a predicate nor a macro.

activities.title: Compare the cost of reversing
activities.prompt: The same edit can run as one `:global` command or as a macro replayed on twelve lines. The result is wrong and must be reversed. What does each cost?

options.label: One undo for `:global`, twelve for the macro

activities.explanation: A `:global` run is a single change however many lines it touched. Each macro replay is its own change, so reversing twelve replays takes twelve undos.

activities.title: Scope first, transform second
activities.body: Use `:normal` for one Normal command across known lines, `:global` or `:vglobal` when text decides membership, substitution for clear textual replacement, `:t` and `:m` when matching lines belong somewhere else, and a macro only when the local edit is genuinely multi-step. Prefer the lowest-risk command that states the intent.
takeaways: Verify the range or predicate before Enter.
Preview a predicate with a search or a counting substitution.
Remember that a fixed relocation address reverses the block.
Test macros on representative rows before global replay.
One `u` reverses a whole `:global` run; a replayed macro costs one undo per replay.
Use `:normal!` when automation must ignore mappings.

reference.purpose: Apply one Normal-mode command independently to every addressed line.
notes: Use a range when the line set is already known; use a predicate when membership depends on text.

reference.purpose: Use `:normal!` and the automatic visual range deliberately.
notes: Mappings stay out of scope; the portability lesson is to prefer `:normal!` when built-in key meaning is required.

reference.purpose: Use `:global` to remove only lines matching a pattern.
notes: The `g` in `:global` selects lines; it is unrelated to the `g` substitution flag.

reference.purpose: Use `:vglobal` to act on nonmatching lines.
notes: State the lines you intend to preserve before using inverse deletion.

reference.purpose: Separate the outer line predicate from the inner text replacement.
notes: A single ranged substitution is simpler when the replacement pattern alone identifies every safe match.

reference.purpose: Combine a line predicate with a Normal-mode transformation.
notes: Keep the Normal command line-local and test it on one representative row first.

reference.purpose: Replay an already-tested macro only on qualifying lines.
notes: The predicate does not make a brittle macro safe; every selected line must still fit the macro's anchors.

reference.purpose: Copy or move every matching line to a chosen address.
notes: `$` grows as lines arrive, so the block keeps its order; `0` never moves, so every match lands above the last one and the block arrives reversed.

reference.command: range, substitute, normal, global, or macro
reference.purpose: Select among ranges, predicates, substitutions, Normal commands, and macros.
notes: Advanced commands are valuable because they clarify intent, not because they are advanced.
